Red List Authority Coordinator: Roslaind Kennedy (email: Rosalind.Kennerley@durrell.org)

documentation.range: Atelerix algirus is endemic to the Mediterranean region, occurring across North Africa from Morocco to Libya, in Spain, and on a number of islands including the Canary Islands, Djerba, Malta, Majorca, Ibiza and Formentera. It was formerly introduced to France, but is now extinct there. Its occurrence in continental Europe and on the Balearic and Canary islands result from introductions by man (Khaldi et al. 2016); introduced onto the Canary Islands in the 1890s (Hutterer 1983, R. Hutterer pers. comm. 2007). It typically occurs at altitudes of 0 to 400 m, although it can reach altitudes of 900 m in Morocco (Lapini 1999).
documentation.population: This species is difficult to record because of its nocturnal habits, therefore there are insufficient data available to estimate population densities (R. Hutterer pers. comm. 2007). However, in general hedgehog populations are decreasing across Mediterranean (N. Yigit pers. comm. 2007).
documentation.habitats: This is a nocturnal and terrestrial insectivorous species; it feeds on insects, worms, snails, fruits, carrion and occasionally small vertebrates (García-Rodriguez and Puig-Montserrat 2014). It has been found in a range of habitats including semi-desert, dry Mediterranean scrub, grasslands, pastures, cultivated fields, and gardens, frequently in close proximity to human habitation. The optimal biotope of this species is open spaces mosaic with plenty of herbaceous and shrub cover, such as fallow or uncultivated fields (Garcìa-Rodriguez and Puig-Montserrat 2014). It is most often found in arid areas (Lapini 1999, Palomo and Gisbert 2002). The reproductive period goes from April to late October in the Balearics and litter size is 1-4 young.
documentation.threats: Threats include accidental mortality on roads (roadkill), (Mouhoub Sayah et al. 2009). Populations may be limited by the availability of suitable habitat (Palomo and Gisbert 2002). The species is sometimes taken from the wild to be kept as a pet (Palomo and Gisbert 2002). It is locally caught and eaten across the Mediterranean region. In Morocco it is used locally for medical purposes and appears in local witchcraft markets (R. Hutterer pers. comm. 2007). Increasing numbers of roads and habitat loss are the most serious threats to the species, although it is unlikely they are major threats at present.
documentation.measures: This species is listed on Appendix II of the Bern Convention, and on Annex IV of the EU Habitats and Species Directive. Surveys and monitoring are required to determine population trends in this rare species. If any evidence of declines is indicated, action should be taken to protect the species. Further research is necessary to determine appropriate conservation measures.
documentation.use_trade: This species is locally eaten across the region and in Morocco it is sold in local markets to supply the demand of traditional medicine (Nijman and Bergin 2015).
documentation.rationale: It is assessed as Least Concern however there are no specific data available for this species and the status of this species should be monitored and more data gathered; if there is evidence of declines in population or range in the future, a reassessment will be necessary and uplisting may be warranted.
